o: Jointness exists only when all members are related through the mother.
Jointness is based on functional unity and obligations, and may also involve common property.
Jointness is defined only by the number of married couples.
x: Karve emphasised functional unity and obligations more than co-residence; she also described the joint family as a residential unit holding common property.

s: Among which groups did Ramkrishna Mukherjee find joint families over-represented?
x: Mukherjee found joint families common in trade and higher occupations, not agriculture and casual labour.

s: Where did I.P. Desai conduct his study of degrees of jointness in households?
x: I.P. Desai studied jointness in Mahuva and identified five degrees of jointness.

s: Who wrote 'The Household Dimension of Family in India' (1973)?
x: A.M. Shah wrote it, distinguished family from household, and gave the developmental cycle of households.

s: Which scholar argued that the family reproduces patriarchy?
x: Leela Dube argued the family reproduces patriarchy; Kapadia pioneered family studies and Shah gave the developmental cycle.

s: In I.P. Desai's Mahuva study, what share of households was nuclear?
x: Desai's Mahuva study found 61% nuclear and 39% joint households.

s: How many degrees of jointness did I.P. Desai identify?
x: I.P. Desai identified five degrees of jointness in his Mahuva study.

s: Who among the following is associated with the 'developmental cycle' of the household, distinguishing family from household?
x: A.M. Shah held that family is not the same as household and used the developmental cycle; Mahuva is Desai's study.

s: Who among the following is regarded as a pioneer of family studies in India?
x: K.M. Kapadia is regarded as a pioneer of family studies in India.

s: On which text did Vijnaneshwara write the commentary that forms the basis of the Mitakshara school of Hindu law?
x: Mitakshara is Vijnaneshwara’s commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, composed in the Kalyani Chalukya court.

s: What did the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act make daughters?
o: Eligible heirs only if the father died after 2005
Members of the Dayabhaga school by law
Guardians of all family property irrespective of descent
x: The 2005 amendment to Section 6 made daughters coparceners by birth.

s: In Vineeta Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that daughters' coparcenary rights by birth apply:
o: Only if the father was alive on 9 September 2005
Whether or not the father was alive in 2005
Only if the daughter was unmarried
x: Vineeta Sharma (2020) held that daughters' coparcenary rights by birth apply irrespective of whether the father was alive in 2005.

s: Who was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, of which the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 formed a part?
x: B.R. Ambedkar was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, which included the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara and Jimutavahana the Dayabhaga, the two classical schools of inheritance; Irawati Karve was a sociologist of the joint family and kinship.

s: The Family Courts Act, 1984, followed the recommendations of which report?
x: The Family Courts Act, 1984 followed the 59th Law Commission Report of 1974.

s: Which Act governs guardianship among Hindus?
x: The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act covers guardianship; adoption falls under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act.

s: Which statement about Andhra Pradesh's succession law amendment is correct?
o: It was enacted in 2005, along with the central amendment
It was enacted after the central amendment of 2005
It was enacted in 1995, 10 years before the central amendment
It was enacted in 1985, 20 years before the central amendment of 2005
x: Andhra Pradesh made its succession amendment in 1985, 20 years before the central amendment of 2005.

s: Who is associated with the Dayabhaga school of Hindu law, prevalent in Bengal and Assam?
x: Dayabhaga is Jimutavahana's school; under it a son's right arises only on the father's death, unlike Mitakshara.

s: Under which 2023 law do maintenance provisions cover wives, children, indigent parents and divorced wives?
x: The BNSS, 2023 contains the maintenance provisions for wives, children, indigent parents and divorced wives.

s: Under the Dayabhaga school, when does a son get a right to ancestral property?
x: Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana) gives the right only on the father's death; Mitakshara gives it by birth.

s: In the court of which dynasty did Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara, live?
x: Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara, a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, at the Kalyani Chalukya court.

s: Under the Mitakshara school, when does a son get a right to ancestral property?
x: Mitakshara gives the right by birth; Dayabhaga gives it only on the father's death.

s: In which year was the Family Courts Act enacted?
x: The Family Courts Act, 1984 followed the 59th Law Commission Report of 1974.

s: Which Act governs adoption among Hindus?
x: Adoption among Hindus is governed by the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956; guardianship by the Minority and Guardianship Act.

s: Among Tiyans, some Moplas and Bants, whom does the tharawad consist of?
o: A couple and their unmarried children
The heiress and her husband, the nokma
The eldest son, his wife and children
A woman, her siblings and her sisters' children
x: The tharawad here is a woman, her siblings and her sisters' children; the husband is not part of the unit.

s: In the Khasi matrilineal system the youngest daughter inherits. What is this practice called?
x: Inheritance by the youngest daughter is called ultimogeniture and is associated with the Khasi of Meghalaya.

s: In the Garo matrilineal system, 'Machong' is the matrilineage. Who heads the household?
x: Among the Garo, Machong is the matrilineage and the heiress’s husband, called nokma, heads the household.

s: The Marumakkathayam system of the Nair tharavad in Kerala was abolished by which of the following?
x: The Nair tharavad followed Marumakkathayam (matrilineal inheritance), which was abolished by the Joint Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. The Hindu Succession Act 1956 is the central succession law, the Special Marriage Act 1954 governs civil marriage, and the Family Courts Act 1984 set up family courts; none of them abolished Marumakkathayam.

s: The matrilineal Khasi and Garo communities are associated with which State?
x: The Khasi and Garo are associated with Meghalaya.

s: In matrilineal systems, with whom does power usually remain?
x: Matriliny traces descent through women, but power usually stays with men; matriliny is not matriarchy.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about changes in family structure in India?
o: Legislation and marital dissolution may bring more separation, single parenting and divorce
Urbanisation invariably eliminates all emotional bonds among members of joint families
Women's employment may lead to more female-headed households
M.S. Gore found that nuclear households rise but emotional bonds persist
x: Urbanisation does not invariably end emotional bonds; M.S. Gore found that bonds persist even as nuclear households rise.

s: What has Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu recently advocated?
o: Replacing joint families with nuclear households
A return to the joint family and incentives for families with two or more children
A two-child limit with penalties for larger families
x: In the context of declining fertility, Naidu urged a return to the joint family and incentives for having two or more children.

s: Which category of urban family is associated with a joint family form and strong elder-male authority?
x: The proprietary class is described as having joint families and strong elder-male authority.

s: Which one of the following changes is associated with industrialisation and its impact on the family?
o: The family changes from a production unit into a consumption unit
The family becomes independent of economic factors
The family changes from a consumption unit into a production unit
x: Industrialisation changes the family from a production unit into a consumption unit and contributes to the economic independence of youth.

s: Which one of the following is a major family-related consequence of urbanisation and migration?
o: Break-up of joint families due to rural-urban migration
Strengthening of joint ownership of agricultural land
x: Limited urban housing and rural-urban migration contribute to the break-up of joint families.

s: Urban families may be studied through livelihood, social milieu, value pattern and which other factor?
x: Urban families are studied by livelihood, authority structure, social milieu and value pattern, not only by household size.

s: Which change in the family is associated with women's employment?
x: Women's employment leads to more female-headed households; industrialisation turns the family into a consumption unit.

s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a factor contributing to the rise of single-parent and female-headed households?
x: Widowhood, marital instability and male migration are identified as causes of rising single-parent and female-headed households. Expansion of joint-family residence is not listed as a cause.

s: High-risk families are best described as families facing:
o: Only economic difficulties such as poverty and unemployment
Only health-related challenges and chronic illness
Only the problems of single-parent households
Severe social, economic, health, psychological or environmental challenges harming members' well-being
x: High-risk families face serious social, economic, health, psychological or environmental problems that harm their members; they are not limited to one kind of problem.

s: Which of the following causes of high-risk families is NOT correctly matched?
x: Debt burden is an economic factor, like poverty and job insecurity; the other pairs are correct.

s: On what has elderly care in Indian families traditionally rested?
x: Elderly care rests on filial piety, which nuclearisation and migration now strain, creating a need for alternative care.

s: Which of the following is a social cause rather than a characteristic of high-risk families?
x: Substance abuse, single-parent households and family conflict characterise high-risk families; social exclusion is a social cause.

s: How did the share of nuclear households in urban India change between Census 2001 and 2011?
x: Urban nuclear households fell from 54.3% to 52.3%; the rural nuclear share rose from 50.7% to 52.1%.

s: NFHS-6 (2023–24) was released by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with which institution as the nodal agency?
o: International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai
x: NFHS-6 was released by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, with the International Institute for Population Sciences, Mumbai, as the nodal agency.

s: What was the urban total fertility rate in NFHS-5?
x: NFHS-5 reported urban and rural TFRs of 1.6 and 2.1; NFHS-6 reported an overall TFR of 2.0.

s: According to NFHS-6 (2023–24), what is India's total fertility rate?
x: NFHS-6 recorded a TFR of 2.0; in NFHS-5 the urban TFR was 1.6 and rural 2.1.

s: Average household size fell from 4.6 in NFHS-4 to what in NFHS-5?
x: Household size fell from 4.6 (NFHS-4) to 4.4 (NFHS-5).

s: Between Census 2001 and 2011, how did the share of nuclear households in rural India change?
x: Rural nuclear households rose from 50.7% to 52.1%, while the urban share fell from 54.3% to 52.3%.

s: According to Census 2011, what share of rural households in India were joint households?
x: The share of rural joint households fell from 20.1% in 2001 to 16.8% in 2011.
